title: Israeli defense minister puts NATO power on notice as Middle East tensions surge: ‘Dangerous adventures’
description: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz warned Recep Tayyip Erdoğan not to test Israel's resolve after the Abu al-Duhur airbase strike in Syria.
fullText:
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz issued a stark warning to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan early Thursday, accusing him of dragging Turkey into "dangerous adventures in Syria" and warning the Turkish leader not to test Israel's resolve.

"Israel will not allow any actor to threaten its security," Katz wrote on X. "It would be better for Erdoğan to continue his detached-from-reality, fanciful rhetoric against Israel in the Turkish Grand National Assembly than to attempt to test Israel's determination to defend itself."

The warning comes two days after Israel struck Syria's Abu al-Duhur Airbase. The increasingly heated rhetoric has put Washington in the position of trying to contain tensions between Turkey, a NATO member, and Israel, Washington's closest security partners in the Middle East. Israel said Syria was on the verge of breaching a security understanding by allowing Turkish troops to deploy there, while Ankara rejected Israel's account.

Syria said there were no plans for a permanent Turkish base or troop deployment, although Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani acknowledged that Turkish military officers had visited the facility for training and exchanges of expertise. Turkey's Defense Ministry said no Turkish military delegation was present at the base before or during the strike, Reuters reported.

Critics Say Turkey's Verbal Attacks On Israel Have Crossed Into Antisemitism

On Wednesday, Turkey called these allegations from Israel "untenable," arguing that they are "intended to legitimize Israel's unlawful airstrikes targeting Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity. ... The imputations voiced stem from Netanyahu's intent to pursue expansionist and destabilizing policies in the region ahead of the elections in Israel," Turkey's government said in a social media post.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee told Reuters Thursday that Washington was working on "a de-escalation process" that was already in place but still needed to be refined. Asked whether the dispute could lead to a direct Israeli-Turkish confrontation, Huckabee said, "I don't think we're even close to that." He said Israel viewed Turkey as "moving further south" in Syria and perceived that as potentially threatening.

U.S. Ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria Tom Barrack sounded a sharper warning after the strike. Barrack said Turkey had received no advance notice and could have prepared a military response after detecting Israeli aircraft heading north toward Turkish territory. He said Washington was working to establish a more robust deconfliction mechanism among Turkey, Israel and Syria to prevent miscalculation or an accidental confrontation.

Sinan Ciddi, director of the Turkey Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that Ankara is portraying the confrontation through a sharply different lens.

Former Syrian President Assad Sentenced To Death In Absentia

"Turkey is chalking up the increasingly escalatory climate between Turkey and Israel to election antics/propaganda by Netanyahu and driving a narrative that Israel does not want stable neighbors and regional powers in the Middle East," Ciddi said.

At the same time, Ciddi said Erdoğan "seems intent on taking actions inside Syria that are perceived by Israel as military escalation," citing proposed arms sales, military training and assistance, continued Turkish influence over former militia members integrated into Syria's new army and, most significantly, "developing military bases with Turkish troops and sensitive equipment."

"Israel established clear red lines about what it was willing to tolerate in Syria," Ciddi said. "Deconfliction only works if parties implement the agreed upon rules."

Netanyahu Warns Turkey Should Not Get F-35s, Citing Erdoğan's Hostility Toward Nato Allies

The dispute was already being discussed at senior levels before the strike. Mossad chief Roman Gofman spoke with al-Shaibani on Aug. 14, four days before the attack, according to three sources cited by Reuters. The conversation focused on Israel's concerns about Turkey's military presence in Syria, including potential troop deployments, weapons sales and drones supplied to the Syrian military.

Attempts to prevent an Israeli-Turkish clash are not new. Turkey and Israel began technical talks in Azerbaijan in 2025 aimed at preventing misunderstandings or military incidents in Syria. Turkey's defense minister said in June 2025 that those contacts were continuing as Ankara trained and advised Syria's military.

Ciddi argued that a mechanism alone would not prevent further Israeli action if Ankara continued pushing against what Jerusalem considers its security red lines.

Trump's Turkey Arms Sale Proposal Sparks Congressional Questions Before Nato Summit

"To the extent that Ankara will push boundaries and attempt to position military capabilities that Israel feels is harmful to its safety, we are likely to see pre-emptive action by Jerusalem," Ciddi said. "The ball is in Erdoğan's court to not raise the temperature."

Netanyahu is also facing criticism from inside Israel. Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak, a longtime Netanyahu adversary, accused the prime minister Wednesday of deliberately escalating tensions with Turkey for political purposes ahead of the Israeli election.

"Turkey is not Iran or Assad's Syria," Barak wrote in Hebrew on X, arguing that Israel's strategic disputes with Ankara could be resolved, moderated or postponed through discreet diplomacy coordinated with the United States.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House, the Turkish Embassy in Washington, D.C., and Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz for comment.

title: Brian Burns: New York Giants' run defense 'dominant' in practice vs. Miami
description: The New York Giants "dominated" the Miami Dolphins in practice on Thursday, says Brian Burns.
fullText:
Spider-Man is unstoppable these days, not only at the box office, where the Marvel movie is crushing records, but on the field with the New York Giants defense.

But that's not Tom Holland out there in Blue. It's Giants edge rusher Brian Burns, who fancies himself after the iconic superhero. He's crushing it, too.

On Thursday, during a joint practice with the Miami Dolphins at their facility, the Baptist Health Training Center, which is located across the road from Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, Burns led a relentless torrent of blue shirts into the opposing backfield.

Brian Burns said the Giants defense was "dominant." They could do better but the Dolphins couldn't stop them. 

Burns was told they had six sacks. He disagreed. He said it was more. pic.twitter.com/dNxcGa9rxX

The Giants have an embarrassment of pass-rushing options this year, so many that stud rookie Arvell Reese is being deployed as an off-ball linebacker rather than on the outside. Burns is the leader of the group that can "get after it."

Abdul Carter, who is on the cusp of possible greatness, mans the opposite flank from Burns. Behind him is veteran Kayvon Thibodeaux. Behind Burns is another very capable vet, Chauncey Golston.

The Dolphins are a rebuilding team under a first-time head coach, Jeff Hafley. They are not expected to win many games this season. They were no match for this group that the Giants general manager Joe Schoen constructed.

Big takeaway in Dolphins-Giants joint practice:

Giants pass rush looks eye-popping dominant. Physical, fast, deep.

Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, Kayvon Thibodeaux, Arvell Reese — hell of a quartet. They just swarm. Jevón Holland had a strong win with 3rd down sack off edge blitz.

Carter is coming, and Reese is on the tarmac. Burns is the star, though. His peers around the league have taken notice. The 28-year-old has recorded 71.0 sacks in seven seasons in the NFL, with at least 7.5 in each of them.

More are coming from Spider-Man.

Rolly Romero opens up on 'dark place' before Ryan Garcia upset, says boxing 'almost tore me apart'
description: Romero enters Saturday's WBA title defense against friend Teofimo Lopez as a man worlds removed from the one who stepped into Times Square to face Ryan Garcia last year.
fullText:
Rolando "Rolly" Romero cringes at the thought. The 30-year-old WBA welterweight world champion won his belt when he did something many thought he was incapable of, upsetting Ryan Garcia in May 2025. Romero has not fought since then, and was waiting, and waiting, and waiting for a chance to defend the WBA title.

Now, he finds himself "stuck," like anyone would feel when tasked with fighting a friend, as Romero is with his buddy, former two-division champion Teofimo Lopez Jr. The pair of eccentric boxing personalities will clash this Saturday at the T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on a PBC pay-per-view broadcast (8 p.m. ET / 5 p.m. PT).

Only the colorful banter that usually engulfs one of their fights will be missing this time.

"Everyone else ducked me, so now I'm stuck fighting my friend," said Romero, referring to Lopez, in an exclusive interview with Uncrowned. "Trust me, I didn't want to fight my friend. It was not on my list, but it is something that I have to do. We do have a history though."

Romero (17-2, 13 KOs) even has it down to the specific dates he and Lopez sparred.

The first time they met was May 23, 2015, at a boxing party. The first time they sparred was February 18, 2016, Romero recalled, when the pair were in their early 20s. Romero was getting Lopez ready for the 2016 Olympics. Lopez (22-2, 13 KOs) and his father and trainer, Teofimo Lopez Sr., traveled out to Las Vegas, to the gym where Romero worked out, and the two went at it.

Romero said that they both had their moments. It was that way in all their sessions, he said — a little of Lopez being up, followed by Romero coming back at him.

"I remember what attracted me to Teo, he was his usual self, and he said something out of pocket that I won't repeat here, but it was really funny and it was offbeat, but not with the intention of hurting anyone," Romero said. "I was able to relate to that, because to a degree, that is me. I mean everything pretty much what I say. If I call someone 'ugly,' it means they're ugly."

The second time they sparred was in October 2016, the third time in June 2017 and the last time was in October 2017.

"I love Teo, but once this fight was made, I decided to go [for it], because everyone else has been ducking me," Romero said. "This is going to be a hell of a fight, but every time I fight, it is a hell of a fight. I wanted to fight after beating Garcia. It wasn't injuries [keeping me out], it wasn't politics. It was everyone ducking me. Garcia ducked me for the rematch. Conor Benn ducked me. [Manny] Pacquaio ducked me. They all ducked me. It's why I didn't get into the ring sooner, although the time off benefitted me."

At that, Romero stepped back and brought up a resonating moment of his career. It was actually minutes before he stepped into the ring with Garcia, who was one of the headliners on Turki Alalshikh's ambitious Times Square fight card.

Romero, a major underdog at -1000 odds on some sportsbooks, stole the show that night, knocking down Garcia with a left hook in the second round. Romero sat on that momentum and rode out a unanimous victory. Yet around that same time, he also found himself feeling "stuck" again, leading into the signature victory of his career.

"I was in a bad place for a time there," he admitted. "I started doing some things I thought I would never do. I have a lot from my childhood that I carry with me, but if you notice, when I got in that classic car in Times Square, heading a few feet over to fight [Garcia], if you notice my eyes, I was gone, lost. I had to kill myself [metaphorically]. It was a hard change. I suffered throughout that down time. I had to kill myself, because I was in a dark place. It's not that I did not like myself, but I had to change.

"I had to find the right way to live my life, because I was living my life like a wild animal. I'm not saying I was doing drugs or cocaine, but I had no right to punch every random person in the face just because I liked doing it. It's not a good way to live. It's just an analogy — I didn't actually do that. But you have to live your life with integrity, and I wasn't living like that.

"Look back at me in that car just before the Garcia fight. No one knows this, but I never beat Ryan Garcia. If it was me, I would have knocked Ryan Garcia out cold that night. I take no part in what happened in that fight. It had nothing to do with me. I know for a fact it was not me."

Romero said it was instead "God" who imbued him with a wisdom he felt before the Garcia fight. He stressed he felt possessed by God before he stepped into the ring.

"When they had us drive to the ring in these cars, God's voice was echoing so loudly in my head that I couldn't hear anyone, it was like I wasn't there," Romero recalled. "I didn't know where I was, or what I was about to do. It's why I had that blank stare on my face driving to the ring. I wasn't there. It was like getting hit by a thunderbolt and I didn't burn. I looked off in the car because I heard God's voice."

It's "God's voice" that Romero hopes will guide him again against Lopez. He was giving away backpacks to his former elementary school when he spoke to Uncrowned. It brought back memories of him getting in constant trouble in school. He could not clearly speak until he was 12.

"It's why I genuinely believe that I'm on some kind of spectrum," he said. "I suppose it's why I can remember specific dates and why I fight. This fight is going to be fun. I know Teo is a good dancer, and I think people are starting to realize that I am a lot smarter than they realize.

"Anything can happen in this fight, and I can't really say what I am going to do and what [Lopez] is going to do. I am settled in my life. Boxing can tear you apart. I know, it almost tore me apart. It's taken awhile, but I have found contentment. I know God is with me no matter what. God will deliver me to where I have to go. It's based on faith and trust. When I fought [Gervonta] 'Tank' Davis, I wasn't ready for that fame or money. When I heard God's true voice [before the Garcia fight], that truly changed me."

title: Senator presses Hegseth, Caine for commitment to keep US military out of the midterm elections
description: Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday to confirm he won’t send U.S. troops to polling places during November’s midterm elections, as Democrats have raised concer...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday to confirm he won't send U.S. troops to polling places during November's midterm elections, as Democrats have raised concerns that the Trump administration could use the military to interfere with the vote.

"I'd ask you to confirm a simple statement: the Department of Defense will not send Federal troops to the polls or to seize election materials of any kind," Slotkin wrote to Hegseth and to Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, in letters Tuesday.

The Pentagon said in an email that it will respond directly to Slotkin, as it does with all congressional correspondence. The Joint Chiefs did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Slotkin told The Associated Press that Trump has been laying the groundwork to claim the midterms were stolen. She noted that Trump contemplated using the military to seize voting machines after his loss in 2020 and has deployed the National Guard to cities against the wishes of Democratic leaders. He also deployed active duty Marines to Los Angeles during his immigration crackdown in 2025.

"He's very clearly laying the breadcrumbs to be able to say the day after the election that he didn't really lose the House or he didn't really lose the Senate," Slotkin said.

Slotkin asked Hegseth during an April congressional hearing if he would follow orders to seize ballots. Hegseth called the question a "gotcha hypothetical," but said, "I've never been ordered to do anything illegal, and I won't."

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles denied in a Vanity Fair interview last year that Trump would use the military to suppress voting in the midterms.

"I say it is categorically false, will not happen. It's just wrongheaded," she said.

Federal law prohibits the deployment of armed federal forces to election locations unless "necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States." If any element of the military were to get involved, it would likely be the National Guard under state control.

In 2020, Gen. Mark Milley, then-chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, responded to a similar letter from Slotkin, then a congresswoman.

"I believe deeply in the principle of an apolitical U.S. military," Milley wrote. "In the event of a dispute over some aspect of the elections, by law U.S. courts and the U.S. Congress are required to resolve any disputes, not the U.S. military."

title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
description: Lawyers for a former Los Angeles homeowner find AI-generated “hallucinations” in State Farm’s filings.
fullText:
Lawyers for a former Los Angeles homeowner find AI-generated “hallucinations” in filings by State Farm.

Lawyers for a Los Angeles firm representing State Farm in a lawsuit involving the rebuilding of a home after a fire have apologized for artificial intelligence hallucinations in their filings.

The homeowner’s lawyers discovered in motions filed by State Farm “cases that do not exist, quotes that do not exist, and holdings that do not exist,” according to a filing by Eric Khodadian, who is representing Fa’alagilagi Meni-Siliga.

Meni-Siliga filed her lawsuit in July 2024, naming a contractor and the contractor’s insurance company, a public adjuster and her homeowners insurance company, State Farm, as defendants.

A fire in her home in Carson, in Los Angeles County, in 2020 caused her home to become uninhabitable, according to the lawsuit. While her contractor was working on the home, a storm caused water damage. After what she said were delays getting State Farm’s approval for repairs, the work on her home was never completed, according to a January court filing. She and her husband have drained their savings and retirement accounts, declared bankruptcy and lost their home to foreclosure, she wrote.

“My family and I have lost forever our family home,” Meni-Siliga, a U.S. Postal Service carrier,  wrote. “We do not come from money… It took many years and sacrifice for our family to purchase our home.”

In its original answer to her complaints, State Farm said negligence by the plaintiff, her contractor and public adjuster led to the injuries and damages she suffered. The insurer also said she failed to bring her legal action within a year of the original loss or damage.

The case is set to go to trial in October.

The legal industry is increasingly turning to AI: 41% of law firms and 47% of corporate legal departments said they are using generative AI, according to one recent survey.

That has meant legal hallucinations have become more prevalent, said Daniel Ho, a law professor at Stanford University who has researched the issue. In one paper Ho co-wrote last year, he and fellow researchers found that a couple of companies “overstated” that their legal research tools could guarantee hallucination-free legal citations.

A database of legal hallucinations around the world maintained by a Paris-based legal researcher has found 1,922 cases so far; most of them occurred in the United States.

Last year, a California attorney was fined a record amount, $10,000, for using ChatGPT in an opening brief that contained 21 made-up quotes out of 23.

Khodadian shared his findings at an Aug. 7 conference in Los Angeles Superior Court. He wrote in a filing later that a State Farm lawyer was “visibly enraged” afterward and followed him and his co-counsel down the hall, “repeatedly demanding to see the list” of mistakes they had found.

That lawyer was Kenneth Katel of the firm Musick, Peeler & Garrett, who in his filing apologized to the court and to the plaintiff, explaining that his co-counsel told him she used AI to help prepare some filings.

“I was not aware that AI had been used, but as lead trial counsel I accept full responsibility for our filings,” Katel wrote. He also told the court that his firm has updated its policy about AI use but did not provide specifics.

Katel disputed Khodadian’s characterization of what happened after the hearing, though he wrote “it is accurate to say I was upset given the seriousness of the allegations.”

Khodadian and Katel declined to answer questions from CalMatters.

The lawyer who used AI in motions on behalf of State Farm, Jacquelene Robinson, wrote in a filing that she confirmed there were seven case citations across eight filings “that simply didn’t exist,” as well as some incorrect titles of cases and quotes that were not found in cases she cited.

Robinson said she used an AI tool called Irys, which she incorrectly thought was tied to her law firm’s subscription to a legal research tool called Westlaw, which she thought “performed an internal cite check.” She was mistaken, she wrote.

State Farm is reviewing what happened, spokesperson Tom Hartmann said. “State Farm expects its external counsel to conform to the highest level of ethical standards and professionalism, including confirming the accuracy of all legal filings,” he said.

Hartmann did not respond to questions about how many external law firms represent State Farm, and whether the company asks about their AI policies before hiring them.

title: Lindsay Clancy’s mother says daughter thought medication was ‘destroying her mind’ as defense begins case in murder trial
description: Lindsay Clancy’s defense on Monday started calling its own witnesses – several of whom described her as a dedicated and loving parent – after prosecutors rested their case.
fullText:
Lindsay Clancy's defense on Monday started calling its own witnesses – several of whom described her as a dedicated and loving parent – after prosecutors rested their case against the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children.

"She always wanted to be a mother, have many children, and I felt it was the best thing that ever happened to her," Clancy's mother testified, before describing her daughter's apparent spiral into darkness and paranoia in the months before the killings.

"She would mention that this wasn't her mind," Paula Musgrove said. "She would say to me, 'This isn't me, I've never been like this before.' And I would agree, because she wasn't."

Clancy, 36, does not deny she fatally strangled her children – Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan – in the basement of their family home in January 2023. But her attorney argues the former labor and delivery nurse should not be held criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and extreme mental illness when she strangled her kids and then attempted to kill herself.

The Plymouth County District Attorney's Office, meanwhile, argues Clancy acted "intentionally, rationally, and swiftly" to kill her three children. Over several weeks, prosecutors elicited testimony from more than 70 witnesses – including Clancy's former husband and her medical providers – as they endeavored to prove she was not experiencing psychosis when she strangled her children.

Through his questioning of the prosecution's witnesses, Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, has sought to portray her as a caring mother who suffered from extreme mental illness and was not properly treated by her medical providers.

Clancy, who has pleaded not guilty to three counts of murder, could face life in prison if convicted. If jurors find she cannot be held criminally responsible, the court will likely begin the process to have her committed to a psychiatric hospital. She is currently being held at the public Tewksbury Hospital in Massachusetts.

Musgrove appeared to grow emotional as she took the stand Monday and described the love she had for her late grandchildren.

"I love my grandchildren with all my heart. And you'll never know what it's like to love a grandchild until you become a grandmother," she said. "It was the most beautiful thing."

Clancy was an attentive mother and a compassionate nurse, said Margaret Hamp, a nurse who worked with the defendant. Clancy would often become emotional when helping strangers give birth, she said.

"She would just say, 'That was so beautiful,'" Hamp testified. "You could just tell that she really loved being in that setting."

Hamp recalled a day early in Clancy's career when their unit treated a pregnant patient who was planning to harm herself.

"I asked (Clancy) if she had ever heard of the Andrea Yates case and she hadn't," the nurse testified, referring to the mother who in 2006 was found not guilty by reason of insanity in the drownings of her five children. "I explained that to her and she cried, and she said: 'How could a mother hurt her children?'"

Clancy was happy the summer after her third child was born in May 2022, her mother testified, but her mood shifted in the fall.

"She told me she was anxious about going back to work because Callan was having trouble taking a bottle and she didn't feel right about leaving him," Musgrove said.

According to a text message displayed in court, Clancy wrote to her mother in October 2022 asking whether Musgrove would stay with her as she struggled with insomnia after taking anxiety medication.

"It's just really scary and I don't want to be alone," Clancy wrote. Musgrove testified she stayed with her daughter for about a week.

Clancy had low energy and "seemed off" around Thanksgiving 2022, her sister Allison Ozga testified, and her condition deteriorated in early December.

"She was having more suicidal thoughts, insomnia continued to be an issue," her sister said. "She was really not feeling like herself."

Later that month, Clancy told her then-husband and her mother she had thoughts of harming the children, Musgrove testified. At the end of the year, Clancy said she was feeling numb, hopeless and had experienced suicidal ideation every day that month, Ozga said.

After a multiday stay at a psychiatric facility in early January 2023, Clancy appeared to be improving, her sister testified. But her mother said Clancy lost a lot of weight that month and became paranoid about things that "really weren't logical."

"She said that she couldn't remember anything. The medication was pretty much just destroying her mind, and it wasn't her," Musgrove said. "She said, 'This isn't me. I just want to feel better and enjoy my kids again.'"

The prosecution's case in chief began last month with two days of heartwrenching testimony from Clancy's ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, who described how his wife's stress, anxiety and other mental health problems intensified in the months after the birth of their third child.

While the Commonwealth argues Lindsay Clancy was not in the "throes of psychosis" when she killed her children, prosecutors have acknowledged she had mental health issues and displayed some diary entries detailing her struggles.

"It's like I'm so desperate to get a mental break from taking care of everyone that my mind is trying to make something physically wrong with me," one entry, read aloud by prosecutors, said.

However, prosecutors said in their opening statement Clancy looked for a "quick and easy fix" for her mental health issues, alleging she sought out different doctors, manipulated her providers and quickly switched medications when she didn't get what she expected.

Dr. Jennifer Tufts, a psychiatrist who treated Clancy over roughly a dozen sessions beginning in September 2022, testified she adjusted Clancy's prescriptions multiple times as the mother of three grappled with anxiety and difficulty sleeping. By the start of December 2022, Clancy was seeing multiple medical providers and had tried "a few different medication combinations," Tufts testified.

The Massachusetts mother asked to change her medications nearly every day, saying the drugs were causing intrusive thoughts, insomnia and numbness, said one of her other providers, Rebecca Jollotta. In online messages read aloud in court, Jolotta – a psychiatric nurse practitioner – told Clancy she believed the problems likely stemmed from postpartum depression rather than the medication.

In a cellphone note last modified in early November 2022, Clancy wrote she was depressed because she was unable to parent her youngest child the same way as her first – an issue she identified as the "root cause of all our problems."

"I feel not as connected with Cal now," she wrote, in part. "I think I sort of resent my other children because they prevent me from treating Cal like my first baby. And I know that's not fair to them."

Clancy's ex-husband said her "big spiral" began when she started taking a new antipsychotic medication around early December 2022. Around that time, she told him she was suicidal and had "intrusive thoughts" about harming the children, he testified.

"She described thoughts of hurting the kids or them having some sort of ailment," Patrick Clancy said, adding he wasn't concerned for their safety because she didn't show "any intention" of harming them.

Lindsay Clancy was "constantly worried that something was going to happen to her children, or something bad was going to happen to the baby," said Letiesha Dukes, a perinatal clinician who diagnosed Clancy with postpartum anxiety in early December.

Clancy called a crisis support center twice that month after experiencing intrusive thoughts about wanting to die, though she did not have a specific plan to kill herself, the clinician said.

During a multiday stay at a locked-ward facility in early January 2023, Clancy reported feeling "numb," according to Dr. Alina Goodheart, a psychiatrist at the facility. Clancy acknowledged previously having suicidal thoughts, Goodheart testified, but said she would never kill herself because of her family – namely her children and her mother.

Clancy seemed to improve after she was discharged from the psychiatric facility on January 5, 2023, her former husband testified, saying he felt "hopeful" at the time.

Multiple witnesses who spoke with Clancy in the days and hours before the killings testified they did not notice anything abnormal about her behavior.

In a telehealth session the day before the killings, Clancy told Tufts she was not having any suicidal or homicidal ideations, the psychiatrist testified, adding she did not notice any signs of psychosis.

A note titled "Medication stole my motherhood and my life" on Clancy's cellphone was last modified the same day, according to phone records displayed in court.

"I was the healthiest, happiest mom," the note said, in part. "I worked out every morning, meditated, and took care of myself so I could be the best for my kids. Until prescription medication stole me from my own body."

On January 24, 2023, Clancy built a snowman with her children hours before she strangled them, her ex-husband said. "She was having one of her best days," he testified.

First responders recounted the grisly scene at the family's Duxbury home, where Cora, Dawson and Callan were found lying in the basement with exercise resistance bands around their necks. Medical personnel described the children's fatal injuries and the desperate attempts to save their lives.

Days later, Clancy was "calm and cooperative" during a psychiatric examination and denied having hallucinations or suicidal or homicidal ideations the day of the assessment, another psychiatrist testified.

Clancy told her then-husband about a week after killing their children she "heard a man's voice telling her that if she didn't do it now, she would lose her chance," he testified. She had never mentioned hearing a man's voice before, he said.

During his cross-examinations, Reddington grilled some of Clancy's medical providers on their care, implying they relied largely on what their patient told them with little independent investigation of their own.

Clancy has filed a civil lawsuit against Tufts, Jollotta and other providers alleging medical malpractice. All the providers previously declined to speak with CNN about ongoing litigation.

title: Ukraine launches 637 drones toward Moscow, mayor says, with Wildberries facility hit
description: Russia's Defense Ministry said it shot down nearly 800 Ukrainian drones.
fullText:
Ukraine launched more than 600 drones toward Moscow overnight, according to the city's mayor, representing one of Kyiv's largest long-range attacks of the war to date according to data analyzed by ABC News.

Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said Ukraine launched at least 637 drones in the direction of the Russian capital from Monday night into Tuesday morning, of which at least 197 were shot down by Russian air defenses over the capital region.

The drones were among 791 Ukrainian craft reported downed by the Russian Defense Ministry overnight.

Andrey Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow Region, said that at least three people were injured -- among them a 10-year-old girl -- amid the drone attacks, two in the southeastern suburbs of the city and one to the northeast of the city center.

Vorobyov also reported damage to residential properties in three districts to the east of Moscow and to a shopping center, local government building and residential building in Kolomna to the southeast of the capital.

Ukraine scales up drone attacks in Moscow, across Russia to record highs, data shows

Another warehouse belonging to the Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries was also attacked to the east of Moscow, Vorobyov said, with a fire breaking out at the facility.

The company said in a post to social media that the "logistics facility" sustained "minor damage" with drone debris hitting the wall of the building.

Mosoblenergo, a regional energy provider, said in a post to Telegram that more than 5,000 customers and 46 "socially significant facilities" in the Moscow region were left without power after the latest round of Ukrainian strikes.

Temporary flight restrictions were introduced at all four of Moscow's international airports, Russia's federal flight transport agency Rosviatsiya said on Telegram.

Elsewhere, at least three people were injured by a drone attack in the Ryazan region of western Russia, regional governor Pavel Malkov said, while three more people were injured by Ukrainian attacks in the Bryansk region, according to local officials.

Ukraine launches 600 drones toward Moscow in major barrage, mayor says

Ukraine has been significantly expanding its long-range strikes deep into Russia in recent months, with prime targets including urban centers, fuel processing facilities, logistics hubs and military sites.

Thus far in August, Russia's Defense Ministry has claimed the shooting down of at least 11,236 Ukrainian drones -- just shy of the record monthly total of 13,312 drones reported in July -- and 34 "Flamingo" cruise missiles, according to ministry statements analyzed by ABC News.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post to social media on Monday that he met with military leaders and discussed "the progress of long-range operations during the first half of August."

"We confirmed the priorities for deep strikes in the coming weeks and in September. The confirmed damage inflicted on the Russians confirms the effectiveness of our long-range strategy," Zelenskyy wrote.

'Trump does like a winner': Ukraine victories could mean more US backing, Zelenskyy adviser says

Russia continued its own long-range strike campaign against Ukrainian cities overnight. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 147 drones of various types in its latest barrage, of which 111 were shot down or otherwise suppressed.

Russian drone impacts were reported in 19 locations, the air force said in a post to Telegram.

One airstrike on the village of Pechenihy in the northeastern Khakriv region killed at least 10 people, according to Zelenskyy. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said that at least 17 other people were injured in the strike.

"We will definitely respond to this Russian attack," Zelenskyy wrote in a post to Telegram."And it is equally important that our partners also support our just and decisive responses with their own steps to put pressure on Russia and to support Ukraine.

In Russian attacks elsewhere, local officials said that one person was killed and 15 people injured in the southern Zaporizhzhia region.

title: Opinion - No, the troops aren’t mentally weak. They just have terrible leadership.
description: Marine veteran Joslin Joseph criticizes the leadership of President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for prioritizing mission goals over troop welfare during an ongoing conflict with Iran.
fullText:
"Mission Accomplishment always comes before Troop Welfare." This mantra was drilled into me as a junior enlisted Marine and has stayed with me well into my career spanning professional sports, project management, and now as a writer. The premise is very simple. You always have to make sure that you focus on completing the mission. No matter if it's a life-or-death battle or something as pedestrian as a corporate product release.

You will have subordinates who always come up with plenty of needs, asks, excuses and problems that they need to deal with. They may have personal problems, financial issues, workplace conflicts, or just have lost motivation to work. And while you deal with all that, you must make sure that you are keeping an eye on the prize and getting you and your team to get the job done. This might make you the bad guy, but let's be honest. If you don't get the mission accomplished, you failed.

However, there is one major corollary to this mantra. Yes, mission accomplishment always comes before troop welfare. But if you aren't taking care of your troops, the chance of your mission succeeding drops substantially. Plenty of military leaders (and business leaders too) have always focused on the first part and completely ignored the second part to disastrous effects.

Enter the USS Abraham Lincoln. Reports of sailors and Marines tasked to the limit on a never ending deployment, plumbing issues, food shortages, and most damningly, being stuck in a combat zone for a war that we have won multiple times according to their commander-in-chief. If you were tuned into military circles, the rumors of terrible morale had abounded since a fire in the laundry room of another carrier, the USS Gerald Ford, broke out and forced that carrier into repairs.

But instead of coming home, President Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and what it's turning out to be a horde of yes-men in the Pentagon's upper civilian circle disregarded military leaders concerns of extended deployments, military readiness, manpower shortages, and the logistics of carrying out an offensive/naval blockade/missile defense/whatever Trump decides helps the stock market military operation against Iran.

Trump proving that he is not the military genius or beloved commander he makes himself out to be seemingly doubled down on the situation saying that their deployment wasn't long enough. Hegseth, a middle of the road military officer, has said that the pictures, news reports, and actual testimonies from the troops were misrepresented.

There is no doubt that the war with Iran that most Americans did not want is going poorly. But it takes a special type of incompetence to be the leader of a military and have a lack of awareness for how badly that affects morale.

Trump has long and rightfully been criticized for his lack of understanding of the sacrifice of military members. His disrespect for military awards, calling the war dead suckers and losers, and fudging the numbers of the war dead from the Iran conflict all stem from the fact that he views them as props.

When he needs a photo op, the troops are valuable to him. When he needs to give a State of the Union address and distract from the fact that the state of the union is terrible, he will march out soldiers and give them medals. A man who has mastered the art of social media deception learned that performative stunts like hugging flags, giving a thumbs up while standing on a grave in Arlington, or saluting a dead soldier in a Trump merch hat somehow convinces people that he actually cares.

But we are at war and the performance theatre of both Trump and Hegseth has gotten stale. We care about our troops being in harm's way and want them not just to be safe, but to be cared for. Military life isn't easy and no one is asking for these troops to be coddled. The troops themselves don't want to be coddled.

We will hear from the toxic vet-bro culture that these issues pale in comparison to what they did back in the day. We will get the veteran pissing contests that sound a lot like how your parents told you about how they walked to school. I have my own stories to tell. But I am also of the type of veteran to know that because I suffered, doesn't mean the people after me have to deal with stupid stuff too. Especially if it could be avoided.

Of course, we forget that Bob Hope didn't do USO Tours to look good for the public. It was because he knew how it affected soldiers to be away from home. There is a reason why mail delivery was important to locations as far away as Guadalcanal. There is a reason why we modernized our food preparation (thank you Chef Boyardee) to make sure troops were well fed. There is a reason why I got hundreds of letters from total strangers while I was in Iraq (I still have all of them).

Trump, Hegseth and their associates sold Americans on making the military more lethal. Instead, they started another forever war and stuck thousands of troops in the worst kind of stress with no support or relief. They forgot that taking care of troop welfare means a better chance of mission success. Or maybe they aren't good enough leaders to have known that in the first place.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary / Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

The Minnesota Vikings received the news they feared Sunday, as veteran safety Jamal Adams is expected to miss the entire 2026 season because of a knee injury suffered during Saturday night's preseason opener against the New York Giants.

Adams sustained the injury during the second quarter in East Rutherford, New Jersey, delivering a significant blow to a Minnesota defense that appeared to have found an important role for the veteran.

For Adams, the injury represents another difficult setback in a career that has been repeatedly interrupted by health issues.

The former All-Pro entered training camp attempting to establish himself as an important piece of Minnesota's secondary. His physical playing style and ability to contribute near the line of scrimmage gave the Vikings another potential weapon defensively.

Now Minnesota must move forward without him.

Losing Adams before the regular season begins creates another decision for the Vikings as they evaluate their safety depth and determine how to replace the snaps Adams was expected to receive.

Preseason games are designed to help teams answer roster questions, but Minnesota left Saturday night facing one it never wanted.

Adams had earned praise from his coaches, built momentum throughout camp and appeared headed toward a meaningful role.

Instead, his 2026 season has ended before it could officially begin.

fullText:
MANILA, Aug 15 (Reuters) - Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro rejected on Saturday China's accusation that he has "consistently attacked and smeared" Beijing, branding the ‌remarks as a "classic squid tactic" aimed at avoiding the issues at hand.

Teodoro ‌was responding to Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, who on Friday said Teodoro had previously led ​efforts by Philippine authorities to apprehend Chinese citizens who, Beijing said, were legally working in the Philippines.

"This individual has consistently attacked and smeared China," Guo told reporters, referring to Teodoro. "What he is damaging is not only China-Philippines bilateral relations, but also the ‌interests of the Philippine state ⁠and its people."

Teodoro, in a statement, defended the May law-enforcement operation at a steel facility in Misamis Oriental that resulted in ⁠the arrest of Chinese nationals, saying it was lawful and supported by evidence gathered through court-issued search warrants.

He cited what he said were violations involving the production of substandard, ​radioactively tainted ​steel, the dumping of polluted water, and ​the release of toxic emissions.

He ‌also accused Chinese embassy officials of intervening in Philippine law-enforcement processes and threatening retaliation against Filipinos, saying a Senate hearing had revealed such actions.

"The latest Chinese Foreign Ministry statement against me is a classic squid tactic - disinformation through avoidance," Teodoro said.

The dispute follows China's confirmation on August 10 that its immigration authorities had taken action ‌against more than 100 Philippine nationals for illegally ​working or living in China. Beijing said the ​operations were lawful and that ​immigration officials acted in a "standard and civil manner" while protecting the ‌rights of those involved.

Teodoro, in an ​August 13 statement, condemned ​China's action against the Filipino nationals, describing it as "plain and simple extortion and blackmail."

The latest exchange continues a deterioration in ties between Teodoro and ​Beijing. China imposed sanctions on ‌him in June after he described China as a "severe threat" to the ​Philippines territorially and politically, prompting Teodoro to respond by calling China "wicked."

title: Grantsville rallies from 12-point deficit, scores 30 unanswered to stun San Juan 30-20
description: For the first quarter and a half against Grantsville Friday, it looked like San Juan was going to remind everyone why it was one of the most dangerous offensive teams in Utah.  Then Grantsville’s defense took over.  The Cowboys erased a 12-0 deficit by scoring 30 unanswered points, forcing seven San Juan turnovers along the way, and held on for a 30-20 victory at Snow College.
fullText:
For the first quarter and a half against Grantsville Friday, it looked like San Juan was going to remind everyone why it was one of the most dangerous offensive teams in Utah.

Then Grantsville's defense took over.

The Cowboys erased a 12-0 deficit by scoring 30 unanswered points, forcing seven San Juan turnovers along the way, and held on for a 30-20 victory at Snow College.

It was a game that seemed to change every few minutes. San Juan came out firing as quarterback Beau Yeomans opened the scoring with a 1-yard touchdown run, and later in the first quarter he found Brigg Palmer wide open for a 47-yard touchdown.

Just like that, San Juan had a 12-0 lead.

And then the Broncos stopped scoring, although it took a while for the Cowboys offense to get going as they threw two interceptions deep in San Juan territory.

But Grantsville's defense kept giving the offense another chance.

"We left a lot of points on the board," Grantsville coach David Millward said. "We had interceptions in the end zone. I think we had four red-zone possessions without points."

Eventually, though, the Cowboys broke through when Carter Bell scored on a 9-yard run early in the second quarter, cutting San Juan's lead to 12-7.

Then late in the first half, Mack Hammond intercepted Yeomans and gave Grantsville the ball at its own 42. Crew Allred immediately ripped off a 34-yard run, and then with 2.4 seconds left before halftime, Allred rolled to his left and found Ty Holm for a 24-yard touchdown.

Suddenly, the team that had trailed 12-0 was leading 13-12.

The Cowboys opened the second half by forcing another San Juan turnover when Palmer fumbled at the San Juan 30.

Grantsville turned that opportunity into another touchdown, with Bell punching it in from the goal line. A successful two-point conversion pushed the lead to 21-12.

Bell added another touchdown later in the quarter, this one on a 7-yard toss play, and Cache Hammond's 37-yard field goal early in the fourth quarter made it 30-12.

That was 30 straight points for Grantsville.

San Juan finally showed some life again late in the fourth when Yeomans found Palmer for a 39-yard touchdown with 5:25 remaining and Randall Black ran in the two-point conversion to make it 30-20.

The Broncos got one more chance when they forced Grantsville to punt, but after driving deep into Cowboys territory, Yeomans threw another interception to Graeson Warren.

That was Warren's second interception of the night and effectively ended San Juan's final serious threat.

For Millward, the biggest thing wasn't that his team played a perfect game. It absolutely didn't. It was that the Cowboys kept fighting anyway.

"I'm just so proud of our kids," Millward said. "They just battled and battled, and we made a lot of mistakes, but they just kept believing."

Grantsville's defense did more than just create turnovers. It swarmed San Juan throughout the night.

"They just swarm and swarm," Millward said. "That's what we like to say, that we just play hard-nosed football in Grantsville, and I feel like tonight, that's what we did."

And that's probably the best way to describe the game. San Juan looked like the better team early, then Grantsville made play after play.

For a Grantsville team that spent much of the first half leaving points on the field, its defense made sure it would get enough chances to eventually make them count.

And when the Cowboys finally did, they didn't stop.

EL PASO, Ill. (WMBD/WYZZ) -- Could this be a state championship season in El Paso?

The El Paso-Gridley Titans were one victory away from playing in the state title game a year ago and have big expectations this fall.

Tanner Benedict returns ten players on his offense and nine on his defense from a 12-1 team that advanced to the class 2A state semifinals.

Benedict's teams are 36-17 and have been the playoffs every year since he was named head coach in 2021. But the Titans had not won a playoff game in that five-year stretch.

"Every year before last year, we had first round exits in the playoffs. The playoffs have been our Kryptonite," said senior receiver Javion Maxon. "Last year will help us this year because now we know the expectations."

Maxon is back after missing the final seven games of the season with a foot injury. Cha'von Maxon and Braden Gibson give the Titans three standout receivers who caught 25 touchdown passes last season.

All-state quarterback Owen Adams returns to lead the potent EPG offense. He threw for over 2,100 yards and 31 touchdowns last season.

The defense, led by senior defensive end Harlin Toillion, surrendered just 11 points a game last fall. The Titans are loaded and hoping they earn a trip to the state title game in late November.

"With how far we went with a young team last year, it just gives us a lot of motivation for this year," said Gibson. "We want a big win at the end of the year, near Thanksgiving."

Roberts started all but one game for the Raiders last year and totaled 90 tackles and six tackles for loss, playing for now-Steelers defensive coordinator Patrick Graham.

Roberts adds much-needed depth to the inside linebacker group, led by Patrick Queen and Payton Wilson.

The Steelers begin the preseason at Acrisure Stadium with a 7 p.m. kickoff Thursday against Green Bay.

title: Defense in Charlie Kirk's killing say shooter should not get death penalty, hit 'intended target'
description: The man charged with killing Charlie Kirk shouldn’t get the death penalty because the shooter “hit the intended target” and no one else was endangered when the conservative activist was shot from a ro...
fullText:
The man charged with killing Charlie Kirk shouldn't get the death penalty because the shooter "hit the intended target" and no one else was endangered when the conservative activist was shot from a rooftop at an event in Utah last year, his lawyers said.

Defendant Tyler Robinson's attorneys say the bullet traveled above the crowd of several thousand people at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10 and "there were no threats to others." Whether the shooting endangered the crowd is a key issue: Prosecutors cited the risk that other people could have been harmed as an aggravating factor under state law that makes Kirk's killing a capital crime.

"The only evidence presented supports that the bullet traveled above, not through, the crowd," defense attorneys wrote in documents filed late Tuesday as the defense tries to block the case from proceeding to trial.

Prosecutors have said numerous people were within a "zone of danger" around Kirk, where a stray or ricocheting bullet could have hurt anyone close to the victim.

The defense lawyers also disputed claims that Robinson targeted Kirk over his political views. Prosecutors allege Robinson told his roommate that he killed the activist because he "had enough of his hatred." But the defense said that was not enough to prove what motivated Robinson, after searches of his apartment, computers and telephone failed to produce anything beyond that one statement.

Prosecutors last month during a weeklong hearing presented what they call "overwhelming" evidence against Robinson, including DNA tests that tie him to the suspected murder weapon and apparent confessions by the defendant.

His attorneys questioned the reliability of the DNA tests and other evidence. They didn't offer any alternative theories for Kirk's assassination, and made no mention of DNA in Tuesday's filing.

Robinson is charged with aggravated murder and has not yet entered a plea. He turned himself in a day after Kirk was killed.

His defense attorneys previously tried to get the death penalty taken off the table after prosecutors were found to be in contempt of court for talking about the case to the media. State District Judge Tony Graf rejected that request.

In documents filed last month, prosecutors said the fact that Robinson loaded his rifle with four bullets showed that he knew he could miss Kirk, "thereby putting others in danger."

But defense attorneys said "it is just as likely that the shooter did not believe he would miss."

Robinson faces possible sentence enhancements if prosecutors can prove he targeted Kirk because of his politics. They contend that Kirk's strong opposition to same-sex marriage and gender transitioning stood in contrast to Robinson, who was in a romantic relationship with a roommate, Lance Twiggs. Twiggs told investigators that he had been considering transitioning around the time that Kirk was killed, according to prosecutors.

Twiggs also told investigators that Robinson sometimes talked about politics, including President Donald Trump. Yet Twiggs said he never heard Robinson talk about Kirk before the shooting. The defendant also did not talk much about gender issues or LGBTQ+ rights, Twiggs said. The AP emailed Twiggs' attorney seeking comment.

Closing arguments in the preliminary hearing are scheduled for Sept. 1. Graf will then decide if the case can go to trial and on what charges. Lawyers for Kirk's family have asked Graf to make his decision by or on Sept. 1 so the case can proceed.

Prosecutors have until Aug. 18 to respond to the latest defense arguments. The Associated Press left telephone and email messages with the Utah County Attorney's Office seeking comment.

Preliminary hearings typically don't last so long. Legal experts said the slow pace reflects a cautious approach by Graf, the large volume of evidence and a desire by prosecutors to disprove conspiracy theories around the case.

New York Knicks reporter expects Karl-Anthony Towns to sign $45 million contract extension
description: Despite not getting the $272 million supermax contract extension from the New York Knicks, Karl-Anthony Towns is likely to stay with the team. Towns was instrumental in helping the Knicks win their first NBA championship in 53 years, playing elite defense against Victor Wembanyama throughout the NBA Finals.
fullText:
Despite not getting the $272 million supermax contract extension from the New York Knicks, Karl-Anthony Towns is likely to stay with the team.

Towns was instrumental in helping the Knicks win their first NBA championship in 53 years, playing elite defense against Victor Wembanyama throughout the NBA Finals.

And even though the Knicks aren't going to sign him to a lucrative long-term extension, the former All-Star is still expected to stay in New York on a more team-friendly contract.

New York Knicks beat reporter Ian Begley spoke about the future of Karl-Anthony Towns, who is unlikely to get the $272 million contract extension from the Knicks.

He noted that Towns and the Knicks have reason to extend their partnership, with KAT likely getting a $45 million per year contract offer.

"If I had to take a guess, the two sides will reach an agreement. Towns clearly loves New York. Maybe he can make more money with another team next summer (Towns has a $57 million salary this season and his contract has a $61 million player option for 2027-28).

"But why would he leave? He won a timeless championship with his hometown team. Unless the Knicks make an insultingly low offer to Towns, I think they get something done here.

"If I'm using the recent Rudy Gobert extension as a baseline, I could see an extension for Towns starting around $45 million."

Begley added that Towns could make more money as a free agent, but with the current financial restraints placed on teams due to the NBA salary cap rules, staying with the Knicks on a team-friendly deal is a far safer option for him.

"By signing this kind of deal, Towns would obviously lose the opportunity to make more money as a 2027 free agent.

"Given all of the factors at play (the state of NBA economics, teams' approach to the second apron, the Knicks' title), there are reasons for Towns to play it safe and sign an extension.

"Towns leaving New York also would hurt the Knicks. If Towns and the team can't agree on a deal, New York would have to make a significant pivot to find another front-line center. So from the outside looking in, it seems like it makes sense for both sides to figure out a deal."

It's hard to see the Knicks letting Karl-Anthony Towns walk in free agency. Despite all the criticism they received for trading for Towns in 2024, he has rewarded their investment with a championship win.

On top of that, he has become a much better defender than he was earlier in his career, thus providing the Knicks with an elite two-way big who can stretch the floor, an archetype incredibly rare in the modern NBA.

The Knicks know that they can't keep their championship core together for much longer, but they should maximise their time together for as long as possible.
