title: Chargers camp day 1: Justin Herbert comfortable in offense, O'Leary's defense flying, & Tuipulotu sits out
description: The Sporting Tribune's Fernando Ramirez writes about the comfortability of quarterback Justin Herbert in McDaniel's scheme and more from day one of camp.
fullText:
El SEGUNDO, Calif. -- It wouldn’t be the first day of training camp without Jim Harbaugh using some sort of metaphor. On Wednesday, he compared the first day of camp to a "family reunion" and "Christmas morning."

Harbaugh is entering his third year building the Chargers alongside general manager Joe Hortiz. Only 14 of the 90 players on the roster remain from the Tom Telesco era.

"We all feel the same thing," Harbaugh said. "It's that feeling like, 'We're capable. We are more than capable.’”

This training camp feels different from previous years, and much of that has to do with the excitement surrounding new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel.

McDaniel walked onto the practice field about 20 minutes before the 10 a.m. PT start. He made his way around to every position group, greeting players with handshakes and daps while spending several minutes talking with them. He was all smiles throughout.

Even quarterback Justin Herbert appears energized by McDaniel and the new offense. While he appreciated the month away from football, he admitted he was eager to get back.

"I thought having a month off was great to be able to go through the iPad and go through exactly everything that we need to," Herbert said. "Guys have picked it up really quickly… So that allows us to be fast out there and go play football."

During OTAs, McDaniel said he wanted Herbert to adjust his footwork by lining up with his left foot forward and his right foot back in the shotgun.

Jessica Cryderman - The Sporting Tribune

Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert (10) talking with offensive coordinator Mike McDaniels during Chargers training camp at the Bolt on Wednesday, July 29th in El Segundo, CA.

Herbert continued working on those mechanics while back home in Eugene, Oregon, where he threw with his brother, Patrick, who is attending the Jacksonville Jaguars' training camp as a tight end.

"You get to the point where you're not thinking about it," Herbert said. "You go out to practice and you're just throwing the ball and now you can worry about mechanics, how am I throwing the ball, where is it going, routes and things like that. As opposed to months ago, it was making sure your feet are lined up with the routes, timing. There was a lot that went into it but now you're just playing football."

The changes to the offense were noticeable from the start of practice, but they became especially apparent during 11-on-11 drills. After Herbert called the play, the offense quickly sprinted to the line of scrimmage and snapped the ball.

On the first 11-on-11 play, Herbert faked a pitch before finding rookie wide receiver Brenen Thompson for a short gain.

Earlier during 7-on-7 drills, Herbert narrowly missed Thompson on a deep ball. The two connected several more times throughout practice, including one sideline throw that Thompson secured with a sliding catch before going out of bounds.

"He's going to be very good," Herbert said. "We saw it early on that he was skilled, he's fast, he's going to make a lot of plays for us. I'm really excited about him."

So far, Herbert and McDaniel appear to be off to a strong start.

The Chargers defense enters the season with several question marks following the departure of defensive coordinator Jesse Minter. The team promoted 34-year-old Chris O'Leary to lead the defense, and players have expressed excitement about working with him again after his previous stint with the Chargers in 2024.

Several defenders have praised O'Leary's aggressive style and believe the unit can remain one of the team's strengths.

"He's not holding back, he's not shy," Chargers safety Derwin James said. "I feel like a lot of people are going to get to see who he really is this year. I'm confident in him."

Jessica Cryderman - The Sporting Tribune

Los Angeles Chargers safety Derwin James Jr. (3) during Chargers training camp at the Bolt on Wednesday, July 29th in El Segundo, CA.

During 11-on-11 drills, backup quarterback Trey Lance attempted a deep pass over the middle, but cornerback Tarheeb Still came away with an interception, the second takeaway of training camp. The first interception belonged to cornerback Isas Waxter, who also picked off Lance.

Still and fellow third-year cornerback Cam Hart are two players James believes are poised to take another step in their development.

"Year 3 is usually when you have to take that next step," James said. "I've been telling him that Year 3 is a pivotal year, not that any year isn't pivotal, but I feel like this is how you shape your career on who you're going to be."

Tuipulotu working off to the side

The only player who did not participate in the first day of training camp was outside linebacker Tuli Tuipulotu.

Tuipulotu worked off to the side while the rest of the team practiced.

It appears to be a hold-in situation as the former second-round pick enters his fourth season after recording a career-high 13 sacks in 2025.

"It's just the process of it, man," James said. "The team loves him. We love Tuli. I knew the team loved me too when I had the same similar situation, but sometimes that stuff takes longer to iron out."

James did the same thing in 2022 before he got his pay day.

Hortiz is familiar with these situations. Last year, left tackle Rashawn Slater held in before signing an extension that made him the highest-paid offensive tackle in the NFL.

Beyond the start of training camp, there was another reason for excitement surrounding Herbert, who recently proposed to his girlfriend, singer Madison Beer.

"We didn't know until after, we were all in the quarterback room and he told us," Harbaugh said. "He had kind of said it was going to happen this summer and everything.”

Herbert and the pop star have been together since 2025. The day before training camp opened, Beer shared proposal photos with the Chargers quarterback early in the morning.

"Man, I was happy for him,” James said. “I was tweeting at like 7 a.m. when I saw it. He told me he was going to do it… So it was fun to see."

Jessica Cryderman - The Sporting Tribune

Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert addresses media during Chargers training camp at the Bolt on Wednesday, July 29th in El Segundo, CA.

Herbert made his first NFL start in Week 2 of his rookie season after then-starting quarterback Tyrod Taylor suffered a medical emergency.

When asked Wednesday whether he was more nervous before proposing or before getting just 90 seconds' notice to make his NFL debut, Herbert didn't hesitate.

"The proposal, for sure," Herbert said with a smile.

Seeing Lawrence coming at him in 11-on-11 drills was a nice reminder to Burrow of the investments Cincinnati made into the roster this offseason to try to reach goals of getting back to the playoffs.

title: Investigators in Comey seashells case omitted key facts and distorted others, defense lawyers allege
description: Federal officials involved in the prosecution of James Comey misled judges, submitted false statements and withheld key facts during the course of the investigation, according to new defense filings t...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal officials involved in the prosecution of James Comey misled judges, submitted false statements and withheld key facts during the course of the investigation, according to new defense filings that seek the dismissal of a case charging the former FBI director with threatening President Donald Trump on social media.

Lawyers for Comey made the allegations of misconduct in motions filed late Tuesday that also call the case a vindictive and selective prosecution, request access to transcripts of grand jury proceedings to expose what they say are "irregularities" in how the indictment was secured, and describe "unlawful" surveillance of Comey by the Secret Service.

Taken together, the new motions, along with an earlier one this week that called Comey's social media post protected speech and not a threat, represent a multiprong defense effort to dismantle a case that defense lawyers say exemplifies a Trump administration retribution campaign targeting one of the president's most vocal critics.

"Ample objective evidence — much of which comes directly from government officials' own public statements and admissions — establishes that the President's animus toward Mr. Comey led to this vindictive and selective prosecution," Comey's lawyers wrote in one of the filings.

Comey was charged in April with threatening Trump through a photo he posted on Instagram a year earlier depicting seashells he said he found on the beach in North Carolina in the numerical arrangement of "86 47."

The Justice Department has said the photo constituted a threat against Trump, the 47th president. Comey deleted the post shortly after he put it up, saying he did not know that anyone interpreted the numbers as a call to violence. His lawyers have said that the slogan has long meant to "get rid of" or "eject" and has been featured on thousands of items sold online and regularly displayed at protests.

Defense lawyers say investigators who tried to prove that Comey intended a physical threat, or knew that the number "86" suggested violence, repeatedly came up empty but withheld that from federal magistrates as they applied for warrants to search the digital accounts of Comey and his wife.

For instance, the FBI searched an internal database of information about open and closed investigations for any indication of an association between Comey and the term "86" but found inconclusive results. An FBI agent also requested a review of the FBI file for the case against reputed mobster John Gambino, which Comey worked on as a young prosecutor, but found no references to the term "86."

Investigators also interviewed a key government cooperator in the case, Salvatore Gravano, who said he did not recall ever discussing the term "86" with Comey or hearing it in connection with the trial.

"Evidence obtained during discovery supports at least a substantial preliminary showing that the affidavits submitted in support of two of the search warrants contained intentionally false statements and material omissions, and that those defects vitiate any conceivable showing of probable cause," Comey's lawyers wrote.

In addition, defense lawyers say the warrant applications distort statements made to investigators by a person who knew Comey but has been now estranged from him for years.

The person, whose name is not revealed in the court filings, is described in the affidavit as saying that they immediately perceived Comey's post to have a violent meaning. But investigators omitted from the affidavit that the person had said their initial impression was that "86" referred to being "out of something on the menu" and only later concluded that it could be understood as a call to violence.

The person said that view was influenced by having listened to an episode of Rudy Giuliani's online show in which the Trump loyalist claimed that Comey had worked on mob cases as a prosecutor in which mafia members used "86" to mean "kill." But the FBI's own investigation determined Giuliani's claims to be untrue, defense lawyers said.

The seashells case against Comey was the second in months targeting the ex-FBI director, a long-running Trump foe whom the president over the years has called a "corrupt piece of garbage" and other epithets.

An earlier case in Virginia accusing Comey of lying to Congress was dismissed in November after a judge concluded that the prosecutor who charged him and another Trump adversary, New York Attorney General Letitia James, was illegally appointed to the job.

Comey's lawyers describe the prosecutions as rooted in Trump's own personal animus, with the Secret Service closely coordinating with the Justice Department and with Trump, who received frequent updates on Air Force One.

As Comey returned to Washington with his wife to be interviewed by law enforcement about his post, Secret Service agents were directed to conduct "unlawful" electronic surveillance, "including as they stopped to visit the grave of their deceased son," his lawyers said. The surveillance had been requested by a senior Justice Department official.

Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's administration. Trump fired Comey in May 2017 during an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's presidential campaign. The men have been openly at odds ever since.

The Justice Department will have an opportunity to respond to the defense filings. The department has not elaborated on any evidence of intent the government has. But acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said earlier this year that prosecutors in every case prove intent with "witnesses, with documents, with the defendant himself to the extent it's appropriate."

"And that's how we'll prove intent in this case," Blanche said in April, shortly after he was elevated to lead the department after Pam Bondi's ouster.

title: How the Jets have built a better defense than the NFL realizes
description: Breaking down the improvements in the Jets defense ahead of the 2026 NFL season.
fullText:
The New York Jets have understandably received attention for the changes they've made on offense during the 2026 NFL offseason, but their most impressive work may have come on the other side of the football.

General manager Darren Mougey and head coach Aaron Glenn didn't simply add recognizable names. They built a defense with a clear philosophy in mind.

Every level of the unit now features a blend of proven veterans, ascending young players, and developmental prospects capable of competing for meaningful roles. It's a strategy that has largely flown under the radar. The Jets attacked the defensive front with both proven production and developmental upside.

Veterans such as David Onyemata, T'Vondre Sweat, Kingsley Enagbare, and Joseph Ossai give New York additional experience, physicality, and pass-rushing versatility. Their arrivals should lessen the burden on returning starters while creating healthy competition throughout training camp.

The front office also invested in the future through the 2026 draft. Rookie edge rusher David Bailey brings intriguing pass-rush potential, while defensive tackle Darrell Jackson Jr. adds another young body capable of developing along the interior defensive line. The second level received similar attention.

Linebacker Demario Davis gives the Jets one of the league's most respected defensive leaders, while undrafted rookies Jaden Keller, Chase Wilson, and Nathan Voorhis provide developmental depth that will compete for roster spots and special teams responsibilities throughout the summer. The secondary may be where the transformation is most noticeable.

Acquiring Minkah Fitzpatrick immediately changes the complexion of the defense. His experience, versatility, and playmaking ability provide Glenn with another proven veteran capable of impacting games in multiple ways. Cornerback Nahshon Wright adds size and depth, while rookie D'Angelo Ponds injects youth and athleticism into an already competitive defensive backfield. Rookie safety VJ Payne further strengthens the group's long-term outlook.

One of the most overlooked aspects of New York's offseason is that these additions weren't made simply to fill vacancies. They were made to create competition. Successful defenses rarely rely on 11 starters alone. They survive injuries, adapt to weekly matchups, and sustain production because quality depth exists behind the first team.

The Jets appear to understand that reality.

Instead of chasing splash signings at one position, they distributed resources across the entire defense.

That's exactly the type of roster construction Glenn has emphasized throughout his coaching career.

Jets Wire will continue to provide updates throughout the 2026 NFL season.

title: Linebacker Dante Fowler Jr. eager to make impact on Seahawks talented defense
description: For veteran linebacker Dante Fowler, Jr., the chance to join the Seattle Seahawks wasn't something he was going to pass up again.  After finishing with three sacks and 15 total tackles with Dallas last season, Fowler signed a one-year contract with the Seahawks in May worth up to $5 million.  Fowler, the No. 3 overall draft pick by the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2015, considered signing in Seattle last year before opting to go back to the Cowboys.
fullText:
SEATTLE (AP) — For veteran linebacker Dante Fowler, Jr., the chance to join the Seattle Seahawks wasn't something he was going to pass up again.

After finishing with three sacks and 15 total tackles with Dallas last season, Fowler signed a one-year contract with the Seahawks in May worth up to $5 million.

Fowler, the No. 3 overall draft pick by the Jacksonville Jaguars in 2015, considered signing in Seattle last year before opting to go back to the Cowboys. But after an aggressive sales pitch from Seahawks veteran and former Cowboys teammate DeMarcus Lawrence, along with a visit to the team headquarters, he knew the time was finally right.

“You can see why they won the Super Bowl, whether it's on or off the field,” Fowler said. “It’s actually pretty cool to see the camaraderie here from the top to the bottom, front office and the team. It’s a great group of guys. You come into this building happy, and you come in looking forward to going to work.”

Fowler is stepping into an enviable situation for a free agent signee, with the Seahawks returning the majority of last year’s dominant defense. Linebacker Boye Mafe (Cincinnati), safety Coby Bryant (Chicago), and cornerback Riq Woolen (Philadelphia) were the most notable losses, but the Seahawks are expected to once again be among the league's best.

Even on a defense as heralded as Seattle, a veteran presence like Fowler can still help make everyone better.

“The way he comes in, he works. I think from a football aspect, like what he’s going to bring to that room, pass rush-wise, Lord, like, he’s able to get off the rock,” linebacker Ernest Jones IV said. “He has so many moves in his bag, and it’s only going to make the guys around him better.”

Fowler was also attracted to Seattle by the presence of defensive coordinator Aden Durde, who Fowler first worked with in Atlanta in 2020 when Durde was a defensive assistant, then in Dallas when Durde coached the Cowboys’ defensive line.

Durde tried hard to recruit Fowler to Seattle last season, and Fowler is excited to once again be working with the Seahawks British-born coach.

“Just to see the way he’s grown throughout his career, and being my defensive line coach at the Cowboys to now his role as a defensive coordinator here, is very awesome,” Fowler said.

Along with Durde, Fowler is eager to continue working with Seattle’s strength and conditioning staff, which he says is the best he’s ever worked with.

Fowler credits the staff for getting him into fantastic shape, which gives him optimism that he’ll have a big year like in 2024, when he had 10 1/2 sacks and 39 tackles with Washington.

“I feel like how it felt when I played in Washington with the Commanders,” Fowler said. “I just knew I was going to have a great season just because of the work that I put in all season, and how good of a shape I was. So I feel like that.”

Head coach Mike Macdonald has already started to feel Fowler’s impact three days into training camp.

“You want to affect the quarterback, but not too much at this point," Macdonald said, “so he’s doing great. He’s getting used to how we roll here, and I think he’s enjoying his time, which is positive. Definitely seeing flashes for sure.”

While he wasn’t a member of last year’s Super Bowl-winning squad, Fowler hasn’t struggled to fit in on a Seahawks team that already has plenty of star talent on defense.

“I just fall in line and do what I’m supposed to do,” Fowler said. “They already had a great defense before we got here, and they won a Super Bowl. It was the best defense in the world last year. So my job is to just fall in line and do whatever I’ve got to do to make this defense upgrade a little bit more.”

title: Kaden Elliss could be the key to Brandon Staley’s Saints defense
description: Why Kaden Elliss more than just another starter.
fullText:
As the New Orleans Saints prepare to open the 2026 season on the road against the Detroit Lions, much of the attention has centered on defensive coordinator Brandon Staley and how he’ll fill the void of Demario Davis. According to New Orleans Football Network’s Nick Underhill, one player could be more important to that transition than anyone else: veteran LB Kaden Elliss.

Speaking alongside Mike Triplett, Underhill explained why he believes Elliss is the focal point of what Staley wants to accomplish defensively.

“Elliss is interesting because I think that he is the piece Staley’s looking at as the straw that stirs the drink a little bit,” Underhill said. “I think he views him as like, here’s my first handpicked chess piece. Like I can do all this stuff with him.”

Underhill believes Elliss’ versatility makes him uniquely valuable in Staley’s defensive scheme, which has historically relied on defenders capable of filling multiple roles. Whether it’s rushing the passer, dropping into coverage or lining up in different spots across the front seven, Elliss gives Staley the flexibility to disguise looks and create favorable matchups.

“I think he opens up the defense and gives them versatility that if he disappeared, I don’t know what you would… I don’t know how that would change,” Underhill continued. “That is a big one because it does feel like he is a little bit more so, positional value aside, like a Jenga block on the defense and that, like if he vanishes, where do you go?”

The comparison stresses just how critical Elliss is to the Saints’ defensive identity, especially following the departure of Demario Davis this offseason in free agency. Rather than simply replacing his production if an injury were to occur, losing Elliss would force Staley to rethink how he deploys the entire defense.

As training camp gets underway, all eyes will be on how Staley utilizes Elliss. If Underhill’s assessment proves accurate, the linebacker won’t just be another starter, but could be the player who makes the Saints’ defensive scheme come to fruition.

title: GOP senators warn confidence in Hegseth eroding as Iran war drags on
description: Republican senators say that confidence is waning in Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s leadership of the U.S. armed forces as the war with Iran drags on without an end in sight. They are also warning t...
fullText:
Republican senators say that confidence is waning in Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's leadership of the U.S. armed forces as the war with Iran drags on without an end in sight.

They are also warning that the success of a possible "massive attack" against Iran could be critical to shoring up support for the unpopular conflict.

Some GOP lawmakers are questioning the administration's failure to anticipate the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz — which has caused oil and gas prices to rise dramatically since February — or failure to anticipate Iran's willingness to strike neighboring allies, such as Jordan, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.

The expansion of the conflict in recent days to the Red Sea, where Iranian-backed Houthi militants targeted Saudi oil shipments, is another troubling development that some Republicans think caught the Pentagon off-guard.

"I don't have any confidence in him anymore. I think he's all over the place — he's accelerating the retirement or forcing out some of the most distinguished leaders in the DOD that we have," Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) told The Hill, referring to the Department of Defense (DOD).

"I think he's got a massive insecurity complex, he has a lack of experience in large organizations, he micromanages too much. He's lost my confidence," added Tillis, who recently has been more critical of President Trump and some of his lieutenants since announcing last year that he would not be running for reelection.

Tillis's vote will be critical to advancing any budget resolution before the August recess to set the stage for advancing a $95 billion reconciliation package that includes $73 billion in funding for the Pentagon and U.S. intelligence agencies.

Tillis says there's a growing crisis of confidence in Hegseth's leadership within the Senate GOP conference as costs mount and Iran appears no closer to agreeing to a lasting peace deal.

"I think there are other people that are probably one decision or another" away from speaking out critically about the leadership of the Pentagon, he said.

One Republican senator close to Defense policymakers on Capitol Hill said that Hegseth is losing support within senior military ranks and that is fueling concerns among GOP colleagues.

"I have heard out of the Pentagon that there's a loss of confidence — within the Pentagon. And of course then everyone here on the Hill hears those same concerns," the GOP lawmaker said, requesting anonymity to discuss private conversations about Hegseth.

The Hill reached out to the Department of Defense to respond to the criticisms from Tillis and other Senate Republicans.

Some GOP senators were particularly concerned over the recent forced retirement earlier this month of Chris Donahue, the top U.S. Army Commander in Europe.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) on Tuesday criticized the departure of senior military officials when Hegseth testified before her panel Tuesday.

"I find this deeply troubling," Collins said at the hearing, which was held to discuss the administration's request for emergency Defense funding. "These are men and women who volunteered to serve our country and swore an oath to support and defend our Constitution."

Collins said after the hearing that she wanted "more information" from the administration on "the strategy and endgame for the war."

"I thought the hearing yesterday was somewhat helpful, but questions remain," she explained.

A second Republican senator who requested anonymity to discuss Hegseth's job security as secretary of Defense said there are "rumblings" about failures to anticipate the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's ability to threaten allies in the region.

"I think there's a sense it's taken longer than what we thought and that maybe our strategy didn't factor in the Strait of Hormuz or [Iran's] ability to be willing to hit their neighbors. I think there was some miscalculations maybe," the senator said.

Nevertheless, some defense hawks within the Senate GOP conference think that Trump and Hegseth can still achieve a decisive victory to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and force Iran to make significant concessions in its nuclear enrichment program by launching a massive attack on the region in the near future.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) is urging Trump to "finish the job" by stepping up the intensity of strikes.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), another hawk, argued that the United States has enough military strength to force Iran to reopen the strait without making major concessions.

"I think we just need to demonstrate our decisive military edge and reopen the Strait of Hormuz because we can't depend on the Iranian regime," Cornyn said. "If anybody can do it, the United States can."

"The problem of endless wars, in my view, is gradual escalation. Until then, you are stuck and there is no way out other than just sort of capitulation," he added. "So I think a decisive outcome by opening the Strait of Hormuz should be the goal."

But there's a general sense of frustration the conflict has dragged out for nearly five months, despite Trump's projection in early March that it would last only four or five weeks.

"I do think that the American public's growing weary," Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) told NewsNation, The Hill's sister network, in an interview.

Some Republican senators think the administration didn't fully prepare them for the cost of the conflict, which Hegseth said last week had reached $37.5 billion even though independent analysts such as Moody Analytics project it has cost at least $132 billion.

"Collectively those of us in Congress are worried about the costs associated with the Department of War and the transparency," said Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

"I think … why they've asked him to come to the Hill and present the numbers, and I still don't know that there's a lot of clarity on that. I think that's what a lot of people are concerned about," she said of Hegseth's testimony before the Appropriations Committee.

Republican senators are warning that right now there's not enough GOP support to pass a new tranche of military spending through the budget reconciliation process as Trump has demanded. The funding would need to move on a special budgetary track to get around a Democratic filibuster.

The prospect of passing an additional $73 billion in military funding to help cover the war costs — something the House approved in a budgetary framework last week — is complicated by the absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), who hasn't voted since June 11 because of a health issue.

Tillis called out the administration for failing to anticipate that Iran would expand the conflict to other strategic chokepoints, such as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which provides access to the Red Sea, if the United States failed to quickly win the conflict.

The North Carolina senator questioned whether the turnover in senior military leadership under Hegseth has negatively impacted strategic planning.

"Everybody knows about some of the Game of Thrones stuff going on with some of the other service secretaries and Hegseth. It seems like he wants to run the whole place," Tillis said.

"When you're a leader, you better damn sure have people smarter than you in the room. You're supposed to be air traffic control for all these brilliant people and he's undermining the DOD's success by undermining these brilliant people who spent their career in uniform," he said of senior commanders who have been pushed out during Hegseth's tenure.

He said that senior generals that left might have alerted the president about Iran's ability to stymie ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz for months or to mobilize allied Houthi militias to threaten shipping lanes through the Red Sea.

title: AI can fuel biological weapons. We must harness its power for defense | Annie Jacobsen
description:

As artificial intelligence rapidly transforms the biological sciences, it is pushing the future of biology in two opposing directions. AI can help bad actors generate recipes for biological weapons with just a few keystrokes and computational prompts. fullText:
The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design

As artificial intelligence rapidly transforms the biological sciences, it is pushing the future of biology in two opposing directions. AI can help bad actors generate recipes for biological weapons with just a few keystrokes and computational prompts. At the same time, AI can track disease outbreaks and deliver critical public health information to millions of people in real time – potentially stopping a deadly outbreak in its tracks. What we are dealing with in this moment is profound: a race between offense and defense. Between the proliferation of dark biology, where deadly pathogens are engineered in secret, and the promise of a new era of collective global health.

Every infectious disease outbreak begins with a handful of cases. Public health wins by learning about an outbreak before it spreads wide, before hospitals fill and a crisis starts to spiral out of control. As transmission rates explode, options shrink. One of AI’s greatest values is its ability to compress the timeline between outbreak and detection. Speed can mean the difference between containing an outbreak and confronting an epidemic, or another global pandemic.

The World Health Organization (WHO) now uses AI to track the spread of infectious disease. At the WHO’s Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, in Berlin, Germany, computational systems leverage artificial intelligence and pathogenic surveillance to track and monitor infectious disease outbreaks around the world. At the center of this new way forward sits a computer-based system called Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources, or Eios (“EE-oss”), which acts as a giant filter for the world’s minute-by-minute health information.

For decades, traditional epidemic intelligence has relied on official case counts. But data from hospitals, labs, research groups and other formal reporting systems takes days or weeks to register and input into official databases. Eios leverages the colossal power of modern computing and social media to get a more immediate picture of a disease outbreak. Eios focuses on unofficial reports, citizen chatter, local news reports, social media posts and more. Proficient across multiple languages, Eios scans millions of websites, feeds and platforms, searching for outbreaks as they happen. It scrapes, filters and ranks information. The goal of Eios is to pull signal from noise.

AI is a force multiplier, changing the biological sciences every day. The real question is not whether AI can do catastrophic harm in the realm of biological sciences – it most certainly can – but whether public health officials can figure out how to deploy AI as a defensive tool faster than malicious actors deploy it as an offensive one.

The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. AI systems can already help researchers navigate enormous bodies of biological knowledge that once required years of specialized training. They can explain complex laboratory techniques, locate obscure scientific literature, troubleshoot technical problems and suggest experimental designs. None of these capabilities is inherently dangerous. Together, however, they lower the barrier to entering what was once a highly specialized field.

The greatest concern is that AIs can help humans create genuinely novel, or new, forms of biology. Scientists are already exploring these possibilities, from mirror-image life to organisms designed with capabilities that do not already exist in nature. Until recently, these possibilities were largely confined to theory or science fiction. Biology is unlike any other technology because what it produces can reproduce, spread across borders, mutate, and evolve on its own. A software bug crashes a computer. A biological mistake can become self-propagating. Once a living organism is released into the world, it cannot simply be switched off or recalled. That biological weapons are alive is what makes them fundamentally different from every other class of weapon, from the arrow to the ICBM.

The race has already begun. As I cover in my forthcoming book Biological War, and this recent New York Times article outlines, biological weapons have an extremely low barrier to entry. Unlike nuclear weapons, which require tightly controlled fissile material and complex delivery systems, biological weapons can be built with widely available laboratory tools, aided by increasingly powerful AI systems.

The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives. The point is pressure, not panic. We need to develop AI systems to strengthen public health, accelerate disease detection and help build biological defenses as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design. Because once biology outruns our ability to contain it, there is no recalling what has already been unleashed upon the world.

Annie Jacobsen is the author of Biological War, to be published on 28 July by Dutton. She also wrote the Pulitzer prize–finalist in history The Pentagon’s Brain and the New York Times bestsellers Nuclear War, Area 51 and Operation Paperclip

title: Patriots DT Christian Barmore has strong message for rest of the NFL
description: Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore has one goal in mind every time the defense steps on the field.
fullText:
New England Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore has one goal in mind every time the defense steps onto the field: to dominate.

The star defender spoke with media members after Sunday's practice, where the top defensive unit got the better of the offense. Granted, the Patriots are still hosting non-padded practices, but the competition has remained intense throughout the first couple of training camp sessions.

"Our goal is to dominate," Barmore bluntly said.

title: Defense tech investors thought the war in Iran could make them millionaires. Instead, they faced a Wall Street bloodbath
description: Firms like Northrop Grumman are struggling on the market despite record military spending. Investors are now watching Congress—and a new generation of startups.
fullText:
The U.S. has racked up a $37.5 billion tab on the war in Iran following President Donald Trump's launch of Operation Epic Fury in late February. Yet despite continued conflict and historic levels of defense spending requested by the Pentagon, investors betting on a defense windfall have watched many top contractors lose value.

How do defense contractors' record backlogs impact future performance?

What role are defense tech startups playing in Pentagon contracts?

Why are defense stocks declining despite increased war spending?

When do defense investments typically generate the best returns?

Trading volumes in major defense contractors surged in the conflict's opening days—rising for some as much as 140% above their average level during Trump's second term—but the gains didn't last. Northrop Grumman is now down over 30%, L3Harris Technologies has fallen over 20%, and Lockheed Martin has declined nearly 13%. Raytheon Technologies (RTX)—No. 49 on the Fortune 500—was at one point down about 18%, though the stock has since recovered to up 4% after the company reported better-than-expected second-quarter earnings.

At first glance, the selloff seems counterintuitive. The Pentagon has fired thousands of high-end munitions during the conflict, including more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles and hundreds of THAAD, Patriot, and SM-3 interceptors to protect U.S. and allied forces, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Replenishing those depleted stockpiles is likely to benefit defense contractors, on top of the Trump administration's push for a $1.5 trillion defense budget—a 42% increase.

Markets, however, have remained unimpressed. According to Guy Rozentsveig, managing director in industries at investment bank Solomon Partners, one reason is simple: "The consensus opinion is that a lot of that good news was already priced in."

Now, investors hunting for the industry's next payday are waiting to see whether higher defense budgets actually translate into new contracts, faster production, and stronger earnings—or whether political and economic pressures slow long-term momentum. Meanwhile, a growing group of newer defense technology companies is hoping to capture a piece of that future spending, too.

Determining whether defense stocks are worthwhile investments takes more than comparing quarterly earnings or even how many missiles are fired alone—it's often largely centered on how much governments commit to spending in the years ahead.

That's why, according to Mike Derrios, executive director of the Baroni Center for Government Contracting at George Mason University, the best returns in defense often come long before a conflict begins.

"Investor 'alpha' is most likely gained when investments are made before wars and before legislated funding, not after a war has begun, become unpopular, or when associated plus-ups are in doubt," Derrios told Fortune.

title: Rams' 26 most important players for 2026 – No. 2: DE Myles Garrett
description: Myles Garrett is entering his first season with the Rams, aiming to take the defense to another level in 2026.
fullText:
Just when it seemed like the Los Angeles Rams were done making moves this offseason, they made their biggest one yet. As the calendar flipped to June, the Rams swung for the fences with a blockbuster trade for Myles Garrett.

They bolstered one of their best positions by adding Garrett, though they did lose Jared Verse in the process. The reigning Defensive Player of the Year joins his best team yet, setting his sights on winning his first Super Bowl.

He debuts on our list of the Rams' 26 most important players at No. 2, one spot ahead of Puka Nacua.

On June 1, the Rams sent Verse, a 2027 first-round pick, 2028 second-round pick and 2029 third-round pick to the Browns for Garrett. It was the biggest trade of the offseason, coming out of nowhere after the Rams hadn't been linked to Garrett at any point previously.

Garrett, the No. 1 overall pick in 2017, spent the first nine years of his career in Cleveland as a member of the Browns, winning two Defensive Player of the Year awards and making seven Pro Bowls.

17 games (17 starts): 60 tackles, 23 sacks, 33 tackles for a loss, 39 QB hits, 3 forced fumbles

Though the Rams run a 3-4 scheme, which would put Garrett as an outside linebacker, they're not going to stray from what he does best. He's still going to rush the passer every chance he gets, rarely dropping into coverage, if at all. Chris Shula will move him around as needed, whether it's to the inside in obvious passing situations or on the edge in base sets, but his primary job is going to be to hunt the quarterback.

He and Byron Young will be the primary edge rushers, rarely coming off the field unless they need a breather. Garrett is also a great run defender with his combination of size and speed, so he'll be an asset in that phase, too.

Garrett has earned a PFF grade of at least 92 in each of the last five seasons, finishing first or second among all edge rushers in each of those years. And by now, everyone knows he set the all-time sack record with 23 last season.

The Rams have had a quality pass rush for the last few years, but since Aaron Donald retired, they haven't had a dominant force like Garrett. He's a complete game-changer on the edge, not only as a pass rusher, but also as a run defender.

His athleticism and sheer strength will instill fear in every offensive lineman he faces, forcing teams to adjust their game plans just so he doesn't take over. That opens things up for Young, Kobie Turner and Braden Fiske, giving them more one-on-one matchups.

He'll have the same effect that Donald did for L.A., only as an edge rusher instead of a defensive tackle.

title: NATO is looking to create the same battlefield feedback loop Ukraine has
description: In Ukraine, data from the front is relayed to the defense industry, which can quickly field new tech before Russia adapts and it becomes obsolete.
fullText:
NATO wants to establish the same kind of battlefield feedback loop that Ukraine has set up.

In Ukraine, data from the front lines is relayed to industry, which quickly develops new tech.

It is then deployed, often within weeks, before Russia can adapt and render it obsolete.

NATO leadership is looking for ways to mirror Ukraine's battlefield feedback loop, in which issues from the front lines are relayed to the defense industry, which quickly fields solutions for soldiers.

US Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who oversees NATO military operations as the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said Ukraine has built high-level contacts with the defense industry "that allow them to innovate very quickly."

Grynkewich, one of NATO's two strategic commanders, told Business Insider at the Farnborough International Airshow in England this week that some allied countries are already involved in these efforts.

For instance, NATO's Forward Land Forces Battlegroup in Romania, led by France, is buying commercial off-the-shelf technology from trusted vendors and immediately testing it in the field.

"So we've got places where we're learning," Grynkewich said. "That's a whole structural thing that'll take some time to adapt across the entire alliance, but we know where we need to go."

Grynkewich said one of the reasons thay he traveled to Farnborough, which showcases the latest in defense technology, was to build what he described as "connective tissue at the senior level."

Ukrainian officials have likened the arms race between Ukraine and Russia to a cat-and-mouse game. In Kyiv, drones, robots, and other new technologies move from the design phase to field testing and, finally, into the hands of soldiers within weeks or months.

Battlefield feedback is quickly shared with arms makers so that they can develop solutions to pressing issues on the front lines. The goal for Ukraine is to innovate faster than Russia can adapt, especially in new drone capabilities, so the product doesn't become obsolete.

NATO leadership has long praised Ukraine's ability to quickly react to the changing battlefield. Some Western officials have said they want the alliance to demonstrate a similar sense of urgency for weapons development and procurement.

NATO isn't driven by the same wartime pressures as Ukraine, but officials and security experts argue that the alliance can't afford to sit back as it prepares for a potential future confrontation with Russia.

The development cycle for complex systems built by legacy defense contractors for past wars — warships, aircraft, and armored vehicles — can take years. However, newer Western startups breaking into the field are trying to more closely emulate the Ukrainian model.

Some war technologies have a quicker innovation cycle than others.

"All the software-centric capabilities are easy to update," said French Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Transformation.

"And so I think we are transitioning from complex-to-update to easy-to-update platforms, intrinsically. That means that the design is now fitted for rapid adaptation," Vandier, NATO's other strategic commander, told Business Insider in an interview this week.

"This is the good news, and I think everybody's going on that. Some are quicker than the others, but it's the global trend," he said.

Because NATO isn't in an active conflict, though, it is hamstrung by regulations and laws that could slow development and innovation.

"I think to match that, we need to have structures that are ready to shift," Vandier said, adding that when the constraints are ultimately lifted, the alliance will be "ready to accelerate."

title: Ukraine's ousted defense minister rejects Zelenskyy's offer of a different government role

fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine's fired defense minister said Thursday he has rejected President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's efforts to persuade him to rejoin the government in a different role where he could continue fighting Russia's more than 4-year-old invasion.

Mykhailo Fedorov, who was dismissed last week after just six months in the job, is a youthful and popular public figure due to his success in modernizing the armed forces and giving Ukraine an edge in the war through innovative use of technology. He has also cracked down on corruption in military procurement.

His departure triggered street protests across Ukraine that have put pressure on Zelenskyy and cheered Moscow officials.

Fedorov said in a statement that leading the Defense Ministry was one of only three jobs that "actually shape the course of the war," along with the presidency and chief of the armed forces.

He said that he would "not accept any position other than" defense minister, in what amounted to a defiant stance against Zelenskyy.

The Ukrainian president said earlier Thursday he had offered Fedorov the position of deputy prime minister for military innovation.

Fedorov said he wanted to finish his reforms at the Defense Ministry, which were cut short after his relationship soured with Soviet-trained commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, who was viewed as part of the military old guard.

"No other role carries the actual authority to combat procurement corruption, complete the army's transformation, plan and execute asymmetric operations against the enemy, root out a culture of lies and unaccountability within the system," he said of the Defense Ministry post.

He said he took over last January with a plan to end the war by improving air defenses and holding firm on the front line while hurting Russia's economy through long-range strikes.

"Our collective results created something unprecedented, a window of opportunity to force Russia into peace through strength. And we cannot afford to lose it," he said.

title: Chaos erupts as House passes $1.15T defense bill with Israel provision: 'Stop stoking Jew hatred'
description: A bipartisan coalition fought Section 219's U.S.-Israel defense cooperation provision, but the $1.15 trillion NDAA still cleared the House Wednesday.
fullText:
The House passed its $1.15 trillion annual defense policy bill Wednesday after a bipartisan revolt over a provision expanding U.S.-Israel defense technology cooperation.

The fiscal year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act passed 216-212, with Republicans largely supporting and Democrats mostly opposing the measure.

The annual bill, which sets Pentagon policy and typically draws broad bipartisan support, received only six Democratic votes as much of the caucus objected to Section 219 and Republican-backed amendments restricting transgender care and easing access to personal guns on military bases.

House Democrats Fracture Badly Over Massie Amendment To Cut $3.3B In U.s. Aid To Israel

Opposition came from a coalition of progressive Democrats and Republican skeptics of U.S. support for Israel, who accused congressional leaders of shielding the provision from scrutiny after lawmakers were denied a separate vote to remove it.

The fight erupted as support for Israel has weakened among House Democrats and some "America First" Republicans during the war in Gaza and the widening conflict with Iran. Just one week earlier, 103 Democrats joined Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., in voting to block $3.3 billion in U.S. aid to Israel.

For opponents, Section 219 would move the relationship in the opposite direction by embedding U.S.-Israel cooperation more deeply inside the Pentagon's weapons-development and acquisition system. The provision would direct the war secretary to designate a Pentagon "executive agent" to coordinate and accelerate bilateral defense research, testing and industrial cooperation.

Critics argued that structure would make the relationship harder for future administrations or Congresses to unwind and could shift parts of the partnership away from highly visible aid votes into less visible technology, procurement and production arrangements. Supporters said it would coordinate longstanding programs and give the United States faster access to Israeli defense technology.

The Us-israel Strategic Alliance – Partnership, Not Charity

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., urged lawmakers to reject the entire defense bill, arguing that the provision would "merge parts of our military with the IDF," referring to the Israel Defense Forces.

"This amendment is an existential threat to American sovereignty and democracy," Ocasio-Cortez wrote on X prior to the vote, referring to Section 219. "Every member of Congress must vote NO."

Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., shot back on X, "Good grief, you are either obtuse or intentionally lying. We are not merging our military with the IDF. As we do with many of our allies, we enter into cooperative agreements, share intelligence, develop technology and ammunitions, and conduct military exercises together. Stop stoking Jew hatred and do better."

Massie similarly opposed both the rule governing debate and the final bill after Republican leaders denied a floor vote on his bipartisan amendment to strike the provision.

"We should not merge our military tech and supply chain with Israel's," Massie said on X.

Beyond creating the executive agent, Section 219 would direct the Pentagon to identify jointly developed or Israeli-origin technologies that could be used in U.S. weapons programs and promote joint ventures, licensing agreements and U.S.-based production partnerships with Israeli companies.

Before final passage, the House adopted two amendments from Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla. One removed four uses of the word "integration," while the other extended annual reports to Congress for as long as the executive agent remains in place. The original reporting requirement would have ended in 2030.

The amendments left the initiative's central structure and cooperative programs intact, falling short of opponents' demand that Section 219 be removed entirely.

Sen John Fetterman Pledges To Be 'Last Man Standing' In The Democratic Party In Support Of Israel

Massie's amendment was backed by Democratic Reps. Ro Khanna of California, Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, Jesús "Chuy" García of Illinois and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan.

Section 219 would not combine the countries' command structures, place U.S. troops under Israeli authority or give Israel control over U.S. military operations. The United States and Israel also already cooperate extensively on defense technology, including the Iron Dome, Arrow and David's Sling missile-defense systems, counter-drone technology and anti-tunnel capabilities.

The provision's principal change would be to place a designated Pentagon executive agent in charge of coordinating and expanding those efforts across the War Department.

House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers, R-Ala., said the provision would improve oversight and efficiency by assigning responsibility for existing initiatives to a single official.

"In no way does it give away command and control of our military operations, personnel or equipment," Rogers said last month.

Critics argued that the executive agent structure would give U.S.-Israel projects a privileged path through the Pentagon and further entrench Israeli technology and companies in the American defense supply chain.

The fight threatened the broad coalition traditionally needed to pass the NDAA, one of the few major bills Congress has routinely approved with bipartisan support. Democratic opposition was also fueled by Republican amendments restricting gender-affirming medical care for troops and military dependents and transgender participation in sports at Defense Department schools.

The House voted 219-208 Tuesday to prohibit Tricare from covering certain gender-transition procedures and treatments, with five Democrats supporting the amendment and one Republican opposing it.

Lawmakers separately voted 221-203 to prohibit transgender girls from participating in girls sports at War Department schools.

The House rejected a separate attempt by Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., to codify President Donald Trump's executive order barring transgender troops from serving in the military. That amendment failed 217-212 after four Republicans joined every Democrat in opposition.

Lawmakers also narrowly approved an amendment making it easier for qualified service members and civilian War Department employees to receive permission to carry personal guns on military installations. The measure passed 215-214.

An amendment that would have largely prohibited Ukraine security assistance failed, though 76 Republicans supported it. The proposal would have preserved funding only for security at the U.S. Embassy in Kyiv.

The underlying NDAA would authorize roughly $1.15 trillion for national defense, including pay raises ranging from 5% to 7% for service members, expanded weapons and munitions production and new investments in missile defense, autonomous systems, hypersonics and other emerging technologies.

The bill would also formally change the Department of Defense's name to the Department of War, deeming references to the defense secretary and department in federal law to mean the secretary and Department of War.

The NDAA sets defense policy and authorizes spending levels but does not provide the money itself. Congress must separately pass defense appropriations legislation to fund the programs and priorities included in the measure.

Consideration of the legislation had been delayed for three weeks by a separate Republican fight over the SAVE America Act, Trump-backed election legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote and identification to cast a ballot in federal elections.

The House approved the election measure in February, but it stalled in the Senate, where Republicans lacked the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster.

Republican leaders revived the legislation through a procedure directing the House clerk to combine it with the NDAA after passage but before sending the package to the Senate. That approach allowed the House to vote on the defense and election measures separately before transmitting them as one bill.

The plan initially collapsed June 30 when 13 Republicans joined Democrats in voting against the procedural rule. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., and other holdouts later relented after Speaker Mike Johnson promised to attach the election legislation to appropriations bills and other must-pass measures.

The combined defense and election package faces an uncertain future in the Senate, where Democrats blocked consideration of their chamber's NDAA last week in protest of the Trump administration's war with Iran.

The debate also comes as the Pentagon seeks additional money to cover the conflict and replenish U.S. weapons stockpiles. The White House has requested an $87.6 billion supplemental package, including $67.1 billion for defense needs, while House Republicans are considering additional military and intelligence funding through a party-line reconciliation package.

title: Will Commanders' defensive overhaul be effective in 2026?
description: The Washington Commanders completely revamped their defense during the offseason, but are those changes going to be effective in 2026?
fullText:
Adam Peters had one major goal during the offseason: Make the Washington Commanders' defense younger and faster. He addressed that largely in free agency, signing players like Odafe Oweh, K'Lavon Chaisson, and Leo Chenal, to name a few. He added to that list in the draft by selecting Sonny Styles with the No. 7 overall pick and edge rusher Joshua Josephs in the fifth round.

Suffice it to say that between the departures and additions, the Commanders' defense looks very different in 2026 than it did in 2025. But will what Peters did actually pan out this season? Under new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones, one of the biggest storylines is whether this defense can get all of its new faces on the same page, something that NFL.com's Grant Gordon wrote about earlier this week.

When you fall from being everyone's NFC Championship Game darling to a 5-12 struggle bus, you can run out of fingers to point. The Commanders put a massive UNDER CONSTRUCTION sign in front of a defense that finished dead last in yards allowed. They used the No. 7 overall pick on Ohio State linebacker Sonny Styles, an athletic marvel who will draw plenty of hype as a preseason Defensive Rookie of the Year candidate. General manager Adam Peters opened the check book before turning in the card to get Styles, too. Washington broke the bank to sign pass rusher Odafe Oweh, while adding plenty more veteran starters elsewhere: nickel Amik Robertson, safety Nick Cross, pass rusher K'Lavon Chaisson, linebacker Leo Chenal and defensive tackle Tim Settle. The Commanders added veteran depth, as well. Binging on free agents isn't always a winning formula, of course. How quickly new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones and Washington's cast of fresh faces get on the same page will be crucial in camp.

If you paid attention during minicamps and OTAs, you already know that the defensive players are putting a huge effort into creating bonds off the field just as much as on the field. It's not a secret that the bond between teammates is equally as important as the skill set each player brings to the table.

The biggest problem the Commanders will have here is the number of new faces on the roster. It's one thing if you bring in a handful of new players to join an otherwise stable unit, but it's another beast altogether when you add a dozen or more new faces. This is the task ahead of Daronte Jones: Make this unit a cohesive group that functions as such.

Jones has an advantage in this, though. The Commanders' defensive players want to bond. They want to get to know each other. They want to work together. They want to win games and prove that they weren't just slapped together haphazardly. Getting the players to buy in is half the battle, and these guys are already there. Now Jones just has to get them to understand his scheme and execute plays proficiently.

US Air Force Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said during a congressional hearing on Tuesday that "recently we had the first air-to-air kill where a Ukrainian F-16 shot down a Russian fighter."

He described it as evidence of Ukraine's growing air-defense capability.

"I think their ability to scale their layered defense has come a long way over the last couple years with the help and assistance of many," he said at a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing.

An effective layered defense employs different sensors and weapons, positioned at varying distances and altitudes, to counter varied threats. It requires not only having enough sensors and weapons fielded, but also the ability to connect them, share information, and assign the right weapon to each threat.

Ukraine has expanded those defenses during Russia's full-scale invasion, combining domestically developed technology and Western weapons with Soviet-era systems already in service.

Caine did not provide details about the engagement, including where it occurred or what type of Russian aircraft was shot down. Some observers have speculated that he may have been referring to a July 8 Ukrainian Air Force claim that its forces downed a Russian Su-35. That, however, remains unclear.

The general cited the growth of Ukraine's defense industry and said he wanted to "highlight the incredible work that the Ukraine industrial base is doing as they scale their own capabilities. It ranges from their surface-to-air capabilities to their air-to-air capabilities." He was speaking in response to a question about what impact a potential US halting of air defense funding to Ukraine for three years would have.

Though it has significantly improved its defenses since the start of the war, including through domestic developments such as interceptor drones, Ukraine continues to ask for any and all air defense support it can get as Russian drone and missile bombardments worsen and continue to threaten both military and civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine received its first batch of F-16s in summer 2024 after a long debate among Western militaries about whether the provision of these fighter jets could be perceived as unnecessarily escalatory and how quickly Ukraine could integrate them and build the training, maintenance, logistics, and operational systems needed to use them effectively.

Ukraine has managed to integrate these assets into its air force, using them to intercept Russian drones and missiles, conduct strikes on ground targets, and now engage hostile crewed aircraft.

And Western partner nations are now studying how Ukraine combines cheap sensors, interceptor drones, dispersed operations, and older flying techniques to strengthen its air defenses and operations.

Partner nations are providing other advanced Western jets to Ukraine, including Swedish Gripens and French Mirages, framing it as both the result of Ukraine's competency and allied desire to integrate Ukraine into the future of Western defense, not just to have it survive this war.
